question: Which statement is true about the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(commission_pct) when run against the EMPLOYEES table?

options.text: COUNT(*) counts every row in the table, while COUNT(commission_pct) counts only the rows where COMMISSION_PCT is not NULL.
COUNT(*) and COUNT(commission_pct) always return the same value.
COUNT(commission_pct) counts every row, while COUNT(*) skips rows that contain any NULL value.
COUNT(*) raises an error if any row has a NULL value in any column.

solution: A - COUNT(*) counts every row in the table, while COUNT(commission_pct) counts only the rows where COMMISSION_PCT is not NULL.

options.text: The number of distinct, non-null DEPARTMENT_ID values found in the table.
The total number of rows in the table, regardless of DEPARTMENT_ID.
An error, because DISTINCT cannot be used inside COUNT.
The number of rows where DEPARTMENT_ID is NULL.

solution: A - The number of distinct, non-null DEPARTMENT_ID values found in the table.

question: Which statement is true about using MIN and MAX on a VARCHAR2 column?

options.text: MIN and MAX evaluate text values in alphabetical order, so MIN returns the value that sorts first and MAX the value that sorts last.
MIN and MAX can only be used on NUMBER and DATE columns, never on VARCHAR2.
MIN always returns the shortest string, and MAX always returns the longest string.
MIN and MAX on a VARCHAR2 column always raise an error.

solution: A - MIN and MAX evaluate text values in alphabetical order, so MIN returns the value that sorts first and MAX the value that sorts last.

question: The COMMISSION_PCT column is NULL for 70 of the 107 rows in EMPLOYEES. What does AVG(commission_pct) calculate?

options.text: The sum of the non-NULL COMMISSION_PCT values divided by the count of non-NULL values (37), not by the total number of rows (107).
The sum of the non-NULL COMMISSION_PCT values divided by 107, treating each NULL as 0.
NULL, because AVG cannot be computed when any row contains a NULL value.
An error, because AVG requires every row to have a non-NULL value.

solution: A - The sum of the non-NULL COMMISSION_PCT values divided by the count of non-NULL values (37), not by the total number of rows (107).

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees;
What happens when this statement is executed?

options.text: It raises an error, because DEPARTMENT_ID is not aggregated and there is no GROUP BY clause.
It returns one row per department with the count of employees in each.
It returns a single row with the total employee count and a NULL for DEPARTMENT_ID.
It returns every row of EMPLOYEES unchanged, ignoring COUNT(*).

solution: A - It raises an error, because DEPARTMENT_ID is not aggregated and there is no GROUP BY clause.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id, employee_id
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id;
What happens when this statement is executed?

options.text: It raises an error, because EMPLOYEE_ID is neither aggregated nor included in the GROUP BY clause.
It executes successfully and shows the first EMPLOYEE_ID found in each department.
It executes successfully and shows NULL for EMPLOYEE_ID in every row.
It executes successfully, because any column can appear in SELECT as long as GROUP BY is present.

solution: A - It raises an error, because EMPLOYEE_ID is neither aggregated nor included in the GROUP BY clause.

question: Which statement is true about the difference between ROLLUP and CUBE when used with GROUP BY?

options.text: CUBE produces subtotal rows for every possible combination of the grouping columns, while ROLLUP produces subtotals only along a single hierarchical path from the rightmost column inward.
ROLLUP and CUBE always produce exactly the same result set.
CUBE can only be used with a single grouping column, while ROLLUP requires at least two.
ROLLUP produces more subtotal combinations than CUBE for the same two columns.

solution: A - CUBE produces subtotal rows for every possible combination of the grouping columns, while ROLLUP produces subtotals only along a single hierarchical path from the rightmost column inward.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT ROUND(salary, -3) AS salary_band, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROUND(salary, -3);
Which statement is true about this query?

options.text: It is valid: Oracle allows grouping by an expression, as long as the same expression is repeated in the GROUP BY clause.
It raises an error, because GROUP BY cannot contain a function call.
It raises an error, because the GROUP BY clause must repeat the column alias SALARY_BAND instead of the expression.
It silently ignores ROUND and groups by the raw SALARY value instead.

solution: A - It is valid: Oracle allows grouping by an expression, as long as the same expression is repeated in the GROUP BY clause.

options.text: CONCAT accepts exactly two arguments; to join three or more strings, CONCAT calls must be nested or the || operator must be used instead.
CONCAT can accept any number of arguments, separated by commas.
CONCAT automatically inserts a space between the two values it joins.
CONCAT raises an error when used with more than one column.

solution: A - CONCAT accepts exactly two arguments; to join three or more strings, CONCAT calls must be nested or the || operator must be used instead.

options.text: It returns EMAIL with every occurrence of '@oldcorp.com' substituted by '@newcorp.com'.
It removes every occurrence of '@oldcorp.com' from EMAIL without inserting anything in its place.
It replaces only the first occurrence of '@oldcorp.com' and leaves any additional occurrences unchanged.
It raises an error, because REPLACE cannot be used on a column that contains the '@' character.

question: A view named EMP_V already exists. Which statement allows its defining query to be changed without first dropping the view and without losing the object privileges already granted on it?

options.text: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW emp_v AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;
ALTER VIEW emp_v AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;
UPDATE VIEW emp_v AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;
DROP VIEW emp_v; then CREATE VIEW emp_v AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;, which preserves the original grants automatically.

solution: A - CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW emp_v AS SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;

question:
View and examine the following statement.
CREATE VIEW emp_v (id_number, surname) AS
SELECT employee_id, last_name FROM employees;
What is the purpose of the (id_number, surname) column list in this CREATE VIEW statement?

options.text: It renames the columns exposed by the view, so that EMPLOYEE_ID appears as ID_NUMBER and LAST_NAME appears as SURNAME.
It restricts the view to showing only employees whose ID_NUMBER or SURNAME is not NULL.
It creates two additional columns in the view, in addition to EMPLOYEE_ID and LAST_NAME.
It raises an error, because a column list is not allowed in CREATE VIEW.

solution: A - It renames the columns exposed by the view, so that EMPLOYEE_ID appears as ID_NUMBER and LAST_NAME appears as SURNAME.

question: A view V2 is created as a query against another view, V1. What happens to V2 if V1 is later dropped?

options.text: V2 becomes invalid, because it depends on V1, which no longer exists.
V2 continues to work normally, because views never depend on each other.
V1 cannot be dropped at all while V2 still exists.
V2 is automatically dropped at the same time as V1.

solution: A - V2 becomes invalid, because it depends on V1, which no longer exists.

question: A sequence ORDER_SEQ was created with START WITH 1. After it has generated several values, which statement is true about changing where it continues from?

options.text: ALTER SEQUENCE cannot change the START WITH value; to restart a sequence from a specific value, it typically must be dropped and re-created.
ALTER SEQUENCE order_seq START WITH 1000; immediately changes the next value NEXTVAL will return to 1000.
The START WITH value can only be changed by a user with the DBA role, using a special RESTART command.
Sequences cannot be altered in any way once created; INCREMENT BY, MAXVALUE, and CACHE are fixed for the sequence's lifetime.

solution: A - ALTER SEQUENCE cannot change the START WITH value; to restart a sequence from a specific value, it typically must be dropped and re-created.

question: Which statement correctly creates a sequence that counts downward, starting at 100 and decreasing by 1 each time?

options.text: CREATE SEQUENCE countdown_seq START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY -1 MINVALUE 0;
CREATE SEQUENCE countdown_seq START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY 1 MINVALUE 0 DESC;
CREATE SEQUENCE countdown_seq START WITH 0 INCREMENT BY -1 MAXVALUE 100;
CREATE SEQUENCE countdown_seq START WITH 100 DECREMENT BY 1;

solution: A - CREATE SEQUENCE countdown_seq START WITH 100 INCREMENT BY -1 MINVALUE 0;

question: A table ORDERS uses ORDER_SEQ.NEXTVAL to populate its primary key. If every row is deleted from ORDERS with DELETE FROM orders;, what happens to ORDER_SEQ?

options.text: ORDER_SEQ is completely unaffected: it keeps generating values from wherever it left off, because a sequence is independent of any table.
ORDER_SEQ automatically resets to its START WITH value.
ORDER_SEQ is dropped along with the data in ORDERS.
ORDER_SEQ raises an error the next time NEXTVAL is requested, because its associated rows no longer exist.

solution: A - ORDER_SEQ is completely unaffected: it keeps generating values from wherever it left off, because a sequence is independent of any table.

question: A user named SCOTT has a private synonym named ORDERS pointing to SCOTT.MY_ORDERS, and a PUBLIC synonym also named ORDERS exists, pointing to a different table, HR.ALL_ORDERS. When SCOTT queries SELECT * FROM orders;, which table is used?

options.text: SCOTT.MY_ORDERS, because a user's private synonym takes precedence over a public synonym with the same name.
HR.ALL_ORDERS, because public synonyms always take precedence over private ones.
Oracle raises an error, because the name ORDERS is ambiguous between the two synonyms.
Both tables are combined automatically through an implicit UNION.

solution: A - SCOTT.MY_ORDERS, because a user's private synonym takes precedence over a public synonym with the same name.

question: A private synonym EMP_SYN points to the table HR.EMPLOYEES. If HR.EMPLOYEES is later dropped, what happens to EMP_SYN?

options.text: EMP_SYN still exists as an object, but querying it fails because it no longer points to a valid object.
EMP_SYN is automatically dropped at the same time as HR.EMPLOYEES.
EMP_SYN automatically starts pointing to the next table created with the same name.
Dropping HR.EMPLOYEES is not allowed while a synonym refers to it.

solution: A - EMP_SYN still exists as an object, but querying it fails because it no longer points to a valid object.

question: Which statement is true about roles that Oracle provides out of the box, such as CONNECT, RESOURCE, and DBA?

options.text: They are predefined roles that bundle together a common set of system privileges, which a DBA can grant to users without having to create the role first.
They must be created manually by a DBA before they can be granted to any user.
CONNECT, RESOURCE, and DBA are system privileges, not roles.
They can only be granted to other roles, never directly to a user.

solution: A - They are predefined roles that bundle together a common set of system privileges, which a DBA can grant to users without having to create the role first.

question: Which statement correctly removes the HR_CLERK role from the user SCOTT, without dropping the role itself?

options.text: REVOKE hr_clerk FROM scott;
DROP ROLE hr_clerk FROM scott;
REVOKE scott FROM hr_clerk;
DELETE ROLE hr_clerk FOR scott;

solution: A - REVOKE hr_clerk FROM scott;

question: A user has been granted a role but has not revoked it. Which statement is true about disabling that role for the current session only, using SET ROLE?

options.text: SET ROLE can temporarily disable a granted role for the current session, without permanently revoking it from the user.
SET ROLE permanently revokes the role from the user, the same as a REVOKE statement.
SET ROLE can only be used by a DBA, never by the role's grantee.
Once a role is granted, it cannot be disabled for any session until it is revoked.

solution: A - SET ROLE can temporarily disable a granted role for the current session, without permanently revoking it from the user.

options.text: It is most useful for queries that filter on DEPARTMENT_ID alone, or on both DEPARTMENT_ID and JOB_ID together; it is less useful for queries that filter on JOB_ID alone.
It can only be used by queries that filter on both columns at the same time.
It creates two completely independent indexes, one on each column.
It is equally useful regardless of which column a query filters on.

solution: A - It is most useful for queries that filter on DEPARTMENT_ID alone, or on both DEPARTMENT_ID and JOB_ID together; it is less useful for queries that filter on JOB_ID alone.

options.text: It allows queries that filter using UPPER(last_name) in the WHERE clause to use the index, instead of having to scan every row to evaluate the function.
It converts every value already stored in LAST_NAME to uppercase.
It prevents LAST_NAME from ever being inserted or updated with lowercase letters.
It is functionally identical to a regular index on LAST_NAME and provides no benefit for queries using UPPER().

solution: A - It allows queries that filter using UPPER(last_name) in the WHERE clause to use the index, instead of having to scan every row to evaluate the function.

question: If an index on a table is dropped using DROP INDEX, what happens to the data in that table?

options.text: The table and its data are completely unaffected; only the index structure used to speed up access is removed.
All rows in the table are deleted.
The table itself is dropped along with the index.
The column that was indexed is removed from the table.

solution: A - The table and its data are completely unaffected; only the index structure used to speed up access is removed.

question: Which statement correctly lists departments where the average salary is greater than 8000 AND the number of employees is at least 5?

options.text: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary), COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000 AND COUNT(*) >= 5;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary), COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id WHERE AVG(salary) > 8000 AND COUNT(*) >= 5;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary), COUNT(*) FROM employees HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000 AND COUNT(*) >= 5 GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary), COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000, COUNT(*) >= 5;

solution: A - SELECT department_id, AVG(salary), COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 8000 AND COUNT(*) >= 5;

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING department_id > 50;
Is this statement valid, even though DEPARTMENT_ID is not wrapped in an aggregate function in the HAVING clause?

options.text: Yes: HAVING can directly reference a column that appears in the GROUP BY clause, not only aggregated expressions.
No: HAVING can only reference columns that are wrapped in an aggregate function such as COUNT or AVG.
No: referencing DEPARTMENT_ID in HAVING requires it to also appear in the SELECT list with an alias.
Yes, but only if the same condition is repeated in a WHERE clause as well.

solution: A - Yes: HAVING can directly reference a column that appears in the GROUP BY clause, not only aggregated expressions.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT last_name, commission_pct
FROM employees
ORDER BY commission_pct DESC NULLS LAST;
What does NULLS LAST control in this statement?

options.text: It forces rows with a NULL COMMISSION_PCT to appear at the end of the result set, even though DESC would otherwise place NULLs first.
It removes rows with a NULL COMMISSION_PCT from the result set entirely.
It replaces every NULL COMMISSION_PCT with the lowest non-NULL value before sorting.
It has no effect, because ORDER BY cannot be combined with NULLS LAST.

solution: A - It forces rows with a NULL COMMISSION_PCT to appear at the end of the result set, even though DESC would otherwise place NULLs first.

question: Which two statements are true about how Oracle SQL treats NULL? (Choose TWO)

options.text: 'Hello' || NULL evaluates to 'Hello', because NULL is treated as an empty string in string concatenation.
5 + NULL evaluates to 5, because NULL is treated as 0 in arithmetic.
5 + NULL evaluates to NULL, because any arithmetic operation involving NULL produces NULL.
'Hello' || NULL raises an error, because NULL cannot be concatenated with a string.
NULL = NULL evaluates to TRUE, allowing two NULL values to be matched directly with the equality operator.

solution: A - 'Hello' || NULL evaluates to 'Hello', because NULL is treated as an empty string in string concatenation. C - 5 + NULL evaluates to NULL, because any arithmetic operation involving NULL produces NULL.

question: Which statement is true about the CAST function compared to TO_CHAR, TO_NUMBER, and TO_DATE?

options.text: CAST is the ANSI SQL standard syntax for converting a value to a different data type, and can often be used as an alternative to the Oracle-specific TO_ functions.
CAST can only convert a value to VARCHAR2, never to NUMBER or DATE.
CAST and TO_CHAR are exactly the same function with two different names.
CAST is used exclusively inside PL/SQL and cannot appear in a SQL SELECT statement.

solution: A - CAST is the ANSI SQL standard syntax for converting a value to a different data type, and can often be used as an alternative to the Oracle-specific TO_ functions.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT employee_id AS id, last_name AS surname FROM employees
UNION
SELECT contractor_id, contractor_name FROM contractors;
What determines the column names shown in the final result set?

options.text: The column names (or aliases) from the first SELECT in the statement; the second query's names are ignored for display purposes.
The column names from the second SELECT, because UNION always favors the last query.
Oracle merges both sets of column names into a single combined header.
An error, because the two queries use different column names.

solution: A - The column names (or aliases) from the first SELECT in the statement; the second query's names are ignored for display purposes.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
SELECT product_id FROM current_promotions
INTERSECT
SELECT product_id FROM low_stock_items;
Which rows does this statement return?

options.text: Only the PRODUCT_ID values that appear in both CURRENT_PROMOTIONS and LOW_STOCK_ITEMS.
Every PRODUCT_ID that appears in either table.
The PRODUCT_ID values that appear in CURRENT_PROMOTIONS but not in LOW_STOCK_ITEMS.
An error, because INTERSECT requires a WHERE clause.

solution: A - Only the PRODUCT_ID values that appear in both CURRENT_PROMOTIONS and LOW_STOCK_ITEMS.

question: Which statement is true about the effect of DELETE FROM employees; (with no WHERE clause)?

options.text: It removes every row from EMPLOYEES, but the table itself, its columns, and its constraints still exist afterward.
It removes every row from EMPLOYEES and also drops the table definition.
It raises an error, because DELETE always requires a WHERE clause.
It only removes rows where every column is NULL.

solution: A - It removes every row from EMPLOYEES, but the table itself, its columns, and its constraints still exist afterward.

question:
View and examine the following statement.
UPDATE employees e
SET salary = (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id = e.department_id)
WHERE department_id = 50;
What does this statement do?

options.text: For every employee in department 50, it sets SALARY to the average salary of that employee's department, calculated by a subquery.
It sets every employee's SALARY to the overall average salary of the entire company.
It raises an error, because a subquery cannot be used in the SET clause of an UPDATE statement.
It deletes every employee in department 50 and replaces them with the department average.

solution: A - For every employee in department 50, it sets SALARY to the average salary of that employee's department, calculated by a subquery.

question: A column BONUS in the EMPLOYEES table is defined as NUMBER DEFAULT 0. Which statement correctly inserts a new row that uses this default value for BONUS, without the caller needing to know what that default actually is?

options.text: INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, last_name, bonus) VALUES (300, 'Diaz', DEFAULT);
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, last_name, bonus) VALUES (300, 'Diaz', NULL);
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, last_name) VALUES (300, 'Diaz') USING DEFAULT bonus;
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, last_name, bonus) VALUES (300, 'Diaz', 0default);

solution: A - INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, last_name, bonus) VALUES (300, 'Diaz', DEFAULT);

question: Which statement correctly renames the table OLD_ORDERS to ORDERS_ARCHIVE?

options.text: RENAME old_orders TO orders_archive;
ALTER TABLE old_orders RENAME old_orders TO orders_archive;
UPDATE TABLE old_orders SET NAME = 'orders_archive';
MODIFY TABLE old_orders TO orders_archive;

solution: A - RENAME old_orders TO orders_archive;

question: Which two statements are true about the difference between TRUNCATE TABLE and DELETE (with no WHERE clause) when removing all rows from a table? (Choose TWO)

options.text: TRUNCATE TABLE is a DDL statement that implicitly commits and cannot be rolled back, while DELETE is a DML statement that can be rolled back before it is committed.
DELETE fires any DELETE triggers defined on the table, while TRUNCATE TABLE does not.
TRUNCATE TABLE and DELETE always perform identically in every respect.
DELETE permanently removes the table's column definitions, while TRUNCATE TABLE does not.
TRUNCATE TABLE requires a WHERE clause, while DELETE does not.

solution: A - TRUNCATE TABLE is a DDL statement that implicitly commits and cannot be rolled back, while DELETE is a DML statement that can be rolled back before it is committed. B - DELETE fires any DELETE triggers defined on the table, while TRUNCATE TABLE does not.

question: A table ORDERS already contains data and currently has no constraint on the STATUS column. Which statement could be used to add a CHECK constraint to that existing column?

options.text: ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_chk CHECK (status IN ('OPEN', 'CLOSED'));
UPDATE TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_chk CHECK (status IN ('OPEN', 'CLOSED'));
CREATE CONSTRAINT orders_status_chk ON orders CHECK (status IN ('OPEN', 'CLOSED'));
A CHECK constraint can never be added to a column after the table has been created and already contains data.

solution: A - ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_status_chk CHECK (status IN ('OPEN', 'CLOSED'));

question: Which data dictionary view would a user query to see the views that they own, along with the text of each view's defining query?

options.text: USER_VIEWS
USER_TABLES
USER_OBJECTS
USER_SOURCE

solution: A - USER_VIEWS

question: Which data dictionary view would show the sequences owned by the current user, including each sequence's current value in the LAST_NUMBER column?

options.text: USER_SEQUENCES
USER_TAB_SEQUENCES
USER_OBJECTS
USER_TRIGGERS

solution: A - USER_SEQUENCES

question: A user has created a private synonym named EMP for their own use. Which statement is true about finding it in the data dictionary?

options.text: It appears in USER_SYNONYMS; a PUBLIC synonym with the same name, by contrast, would appear in ALL_SYNONYMS with PUBLIC listed as the owner.
Private synonyms never appear in any data dictionary view.
It only appears in DBA_SYNONYMS, never in a view the synonym's own creator can query.
USER_SYNONYMS lists only public synonyms, never private ones.

solution: A - It appears in USER_SYNONYMS; a PUBLIC synonym with the same name, by contrast, would appear in ALL_SYNONYMS with PUBLIC listed as the owner.

question: Which statement correctly removes the SELECT privilege on the ORDERS table from the user HR, assuming SCOTT originally granted it?

options.text: REVOKE SELECT ON orders FROM hr;
REVOKE SELECT FROM orders ON hr;
DELETE SELECT ON orders FROM hr;
DROP PRIVILEGE SELECT ON orders FROM hr;

solution: A - REVOKE SELECT ON orders FROM hr;

options.text: Every user in the database is able to SELECT from ORDERS, not just a specific named user or role.
The privilege is granted only to users who are currently connected to the database.
PUBLIC is treated as the name of a specific role that must be created before this statement can succeed.
GRANT ... TO PUBLIC has no practical effect and is simply ignored by Oracle.
